messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor node load ($R_L$) from a piezo transducer.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $v_{avg} \ge 1.8$ V (S1-S6)
        *   $v_{max} \le 3.6$ V (S1-S6)
        *   $v_{pp} \le 0.05$ V (S1-S6)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4$ s (S1-S6)
        *   $dv \le 0.02$ V (S1-S6)
    *   Piezo Model: Current source $I_p \sin(2\pi ft)$ in parallel with $C_p$ (25 nF) and $R_{leak}$ (20 M$\Omega$).
    *   Operating Conditions: Varying $I_p$, $f$, $C_p$, and $R_L$.
    *   Key Issues with FBR (Full-Bridge Rectifier):
        *   S2 (Heavy load): $v_{avg} = 1.76$ V (Too low).
        *   S3 (Strong excitation, light load): $v_{max} = 5.72$ V (Too high, exceeds 3.6 V).
        *   S4 (Weak excitation): $v_{avg} = 1.51$ V (Too low).
        *   S5 (Low freq): $dv$ failure (Settling time issue).

    *   The FBR is passive. It's simple but inefficient for low open-circuit voltages ($V_{OC} \approx 3.2$ V). Diode drops (0.25 V x 2 = 0.5 V) are significant.
    *   To improve $v_{avg}$ (S2, S4), we need a way to extract more energy or reduce the voltage drop.
    *   To prevent $v_{max} > 3.6$ V (S3), we need a clamping mechanism (Zener diode).
    *   To reduce $v_{pp}$ and improve stability ($dv$), a larger storage capacitor $C_{out}$ is needed, but it might slow down $t_{up}$.

    *   *SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor):* Uses a switch and inductor to flip the voltage across $C_p$ at peaks, significantly increasing the extracted power.
    *   *Parallel-SSHI or Modified SSHI:* Variations to optimize for specific conditions.
    *   *Active Rectification (Synchronous Rectification):* Replacing diodes with switches to eliminate $V_f$. (Though the `SYNC` controller here is primarily designed for L-Cp inversion).
    *   *Zener Clamp:* Crucial for S3.

    *   **Design 1: FBR with Zener Clamp (The "Safe" Baseline)**
        *   Basically FBR but adding a DZ33 diode from `out` to `0` to handle S3. This doesn't fix S2/S4 but it's a starting point. Actually, let's try to be more ambitious.

    *   **Design 2: SSHI-like (L-Cp Inversion) with FBR**
        *   Topology: Piezo $\to$ L-C inversion circuit $\to$ Full Bridge $\to$ C-out.
        *   Actually, the common SSHI consists of a rectifier and an inductor-switch combination that acts on the piezo capacitance.
        *   *Standard SSHI:* Piezo $\to$ Bridge $\to$ Out. Switch/Inductor flip the voltage *across the piezo*.
        *   Wait, the `SYNC` controller description: "closes its switches for 'ton' seconds ... at the piezo voltage extrema ... For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp)". This suggests a specific intended use:
            *   Piezo $pzp$ and $pzn$.
            *   Inductor $L$ and switch $S$ connected in a way that they short the piezo (through $L$) at the peaks to invert the charge.
            *   Simultaneously, the charge is pushed into the storage capacitor.

    *   **Design 3: Synchronous Rectification / Boost-like approach?**
        *   Given the components (SYNC, S, L, D, C), a simple and effective approach is the "Parallel-SSHI" or a modified bridge.

    *   Let's look at the "L-Cp inversion" hint.
        *   If we connect an inductor $L$ and a switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo (between $pzp$ and $pzn$), when the switch closes, $C_p$ and $L$ form a resonant circuit, flipping the voltage $V_{pzp} - V_{pzn}$.
        *   But how does the energy get to the output? We still need a rectifier.
        *   Circuit:
            1. Piezo ($pzp, pzn$).
            2. Bridge Rectifier from ($pzp, pzn$) to ($out, 0$).
            3. Inversion circuit: $L$ and $S$ (controlled by SYNC) in parallel with the piezo terminals.
            4. Storage capacitor $C_{out}$ at $out$.
            5. Zener $DZ33$ at $out$ to cap the voltage at 3.3V.

    *   *Refining Design 2 (SSHI + FBR + Zener):*
        *   Components:
            *   D1-D4: DSCH Full Bridge.
            *   L1: Inductor.
            *   S1: Switch (ctrl: G1).
            *   G1: SYNC (edges: both, ton: approx $\pi\sqrt{LC_p}$).
            *   C1: Storage capacitor.
            *   D5: DZ33 (out to 0).
        *   *Wait*, if the switch $S1$ and $L1$ are directly across $pzp$ and $pzn$, it will invert the voltage, but the bridge will still rectify it. This is the essence of SSHI.

    *   *Wait, look at the Reference Design again.* It was just a bridge. It failed S2, S3, S4.
        *   S2 (heavy load) $\to$ needs more power.
        *   S3 (light load) $\to$ needs voltage clamping.
        *   S4 (weak excitation) $\to$ needs more power.
        *   SSHI increases power extraction. Zener limits $v_{max}$.

    *   *Alternative Topology (Half-bridge/Single-ended SSHI):*
        *   If $pzn$ is grounded, we can use a simpler circuit. But $pzn$ is not necessarily grounded in the test bench.
        *   Let's stick to the Full-Bridge + Inversion.

    *   *Let's try a second, different approach: Synchronous Rectification (using switches instead of diodes).*
        *   If we use switches for rectification, we remove the 0.5V drop.
        *   S1: `pzp` to `out`
        *   S2: `pzn` to `out`
        *   S3: `0` to `pzp`
        *   S4: `0` to `pzn`
        *   This would require 4 switches and 2 SYNCs (since we only have 2 SYNCs).
        *   Actually, we can't do a full synchronous bridge with only 2 SYNCs.
        *   Maybe a half-wave synchronous rectifier? Or a bridge with 2 diodes and 2 switches?
        *   Diode $D1(0 \to pzp)$, Diode $D2(0 \to pzn)$.
        *   Switch $S1(pzp \to out)$, Switch $S2(pzn \to out)$.
        *   SYNC G1: `edges: pos`, `ctrl: S1`.
        *   SYNC G2: `edges: neg`, `ctrl: S2`.
        *   This removes the diode drop on the high side.

    *   *Comparing SSHI vs. Synchronous Rectification:*
        *   SSHI is generally more powerful for piezo because it overcomes the $C_p$ voltage limit.
        *   Let's propose one SSHI-based and one Synchronous Rectification-based (or hybrid).

    *   **Proposal 1: SSHI + FBR + Zener (The "Power" approach)**
        *   FBR (D1-D4, DSCH)
        *   C_out (C1, 2.2uF)
        *   DZ33 (D5, out to 0)
        *   L1 + S1 (S1 ctrl by G1, both edges) in parallel with piezo.
        *   G1 (SYNC, ton $\approx \pi\sqrt{L C_p}$).
        *   *Rationale:* SSHI increases power to fix S2/S4; Zener fixes S3.

    *   **Proposal 2: Synchronous Half-Bridge + Zener (The "Low Drop" approach)**
        *   S1 (pzp to out, G1 pos), S2 (pzn to out, G2 neg).
        *   D1 (0 to pzp, DSCH), D2 (0 to pzn, DSCH).
        *   C1 (out to 0).
        *   D3 (out to 0, DZ33).
        *   *Rationale:* Reduces diode drops to improve $v_{avg}$ for S2/S4. Zener fixes S3.

    *   **Proposal 3: Simplified SSHI (Single-ended) with Zener**
        *   L1, S1, D1, C1, DZ33.
        *   L1 from pzp to n1, S1 from n1 to 0, D1 from n1 to out? No, that's not right.
        *   Let's try a "Cold-start" friendly bridge with a larger capacitor and a Zener.
        *   Actually, let's stick to the most robust ones.

    *   Wait, the `S` switch `Ron` is 2 Ohm. The `SYNC` controller is ideal.
    *   For SSHI, $L$ should be around $10-100 \mu\text{H}$. $\pi\sqrt{25\text{nF} \cdot 22\mu\text{H}} \approx 16 \mu\text{s}$.
    *   Let's refine Proposal 1 (SSHI).

    *   *Wait*, there's a detail: "at most 16 components".
        *   D1, D2, D3, D4 (Bridge) - 4
        *   S1, L1 (Inversion) - 2
        *   G1 (SYNC) - 1
        *   C1 (Storage) - 1
        *   D5 (Zener) - 1
        *   Total: 9 components. This is well within the limit.

    *   *Refining Proposal 2 (Synchronous Rectification):*
        *   S1, S2 (Switches) - 2
        *   G1, G2 (SYNCs) - 2
        *   D1, D2 (Diodes) - 2
        *   C1 (Storage) - 1
        *   D3 (Zener) - 1
        *   Total: 8 components.

    *   *Self-Correction on SSHI:* In a standard SSHI, the switch $S$ is in parallel with the piezo. But it often uses a capacitor $C_{fly}$ to avoid direct shorting. However, the "L-Cp inversion" hint specifically mentions $\pi\sqrt{LC_p}$. This implies a direct resonant inversion.

    *   *Let's think about the Zener again.* DZ33 is a 3.3 V Zener. $v_{max} \le 3.6$ V. So DZ33 should work well.

    *   *One more check on the FBR Reference Design failures:*
        *   S2: $v_{avg}=1.76$ (below 1.8). Needs more efficiency/power.
        *   S3: $v_{max}=5.72$ (above 3.6). Needs clamping.
        *   S4: $v_{avg}=1.51$ (below 1.8). Needs more efficiency/power.
        *   S5: $dv$ fail (settled mean changes). This is usually a stability/time constant issue (C_out too small or too large).

    *   Let's go with:
        1.  **SSHI + FBR + Zener** (Focus: Power boost + Clamping)
        2.  **Synchronous Bridge + Zener** (Focus: Low drop + Clamping)
        3.  **Passive Bridge + Zener + High C_out** (Focus: Clamping + Stability, though likely to fail S2/S4 again, it's a control) - No, better to try a **Boost-based** if possible, but we don't have a PWM controller, only a SYNC controller.

    *   Wait, the SYNC controller is for "piezo voltage extrema". This is exactly what SSHI uses.

    *   Let's double-check the SYNC controller's logic:
        *   "closes its switches for 'ton' seconds... at the piezo voltage extrema... edges: both, pos, neg".
        *   For SSHI, we want it to close at both the positive and negative peaks of the piezo voltage to flip the charge.

    *   *Circuit for SSHI:*
        *   Piezo (pzp, pzn).
        *   D1: pzp -> out, D2: pzn -> out, D3: 0 -> pzp, D4: 0 -> pzn.
        *   L1: pzp -> n1.
        *   S1: n1 -> pzn.
        *   G1: SYNC (ton=... , edges=both).

    *   *Circuit for Synchronous Rectifier:*
        *   S1: pzp -> out (G1 pos).
        *   S2: pzn -> out (G2 neg).
        *   D1: 0 -> pzp.
        *   D2: 0 -> pzn.
        *   D3: out -> 0 (Zener).
        *   C1: out -> 0.

    *   Wait, the "S" component `Ron` is 2 Ohm. For the Synchronous Rectifier, this is much better than a diode drop of 0.25V at low currents.

    *   *Wait*, one more thing. The "L-Cp inversion" hint says $t_{on} \approx \pi\sqrt{LC_p}$.
        If $L = 100 \mu\text{H}$ and $C_p = 25 \text{nF}$, $t_{on} \approx \pi\sqrt{2.5 \cdot 10^{-9}} \approx 50 \mu\text{s}$.
        The `ton` range is $10^{-7}$ to $0.001$ s. This fits.

    *   *Let's refine the Zener for both.* DZ33. Nodes: `["0", "out"]`. (Cathode on out).

    *   *Wait*, in the Synchronous Rectifier (Proposal 2), the switches S1 and S2 are `pzp -> out` and `pzn -> out`.
        When G1 (pos) closes S1, $V_{out} = V_{pzp}$.
        When G2 (neg) closes S2, $V_{out} = V_{pzn}$.
        This is like a half-bridge.
        To make it a full bridge, we need to connect the other side.
        If we have D1 (0 -> pzp) and D2 (0 -> pzn), then:
        - During positive peak: $pzp$ is high, $pzn$ is low. S1 closes, $pzp \to out$. D2 conducts, $0 \to pzn$.
        - During negative peak: $pzn$ is high, $pzp$ is low. S2 closes, $pzn \to out$. D1 conducts, $0 \to pzp$.
        This is exactly a rectifier where the "top" diodes are replaced by switches. This reduces the drop from $2 \times 0.25\text{V}$ to $1 \times 0.25\text{V} + I \times 2\Omega$.

    *   *Final check on components:*
        - Proposal 1: L1, S1, G1, D1, D2, D3, D4, D5, C1. (9 components)
        - Proposal 2: S1, S2, G1, G2, D1, D2, D3, C1. (8 components)

    *   *Let's add a third: A modified SSHI* where we only invert on one edge to see if it helps stability? No, "both" is standard. Let's try a version of Proposal 1 without the full bridge, but a half-bridge, to save components and see if it works? No, the piezo is floating. Full bridge is necessary.

    *   Actually, let's try a "Capacitive SSHI" if possible? No, we have $L$.

    *   Wait, for the Synchronous Rectifier, if I use `edges: pos` for S1 and `edges: neg` for S2, I should set `phase: 0`.

    *   Let's refine the values for the initial proposal (they will be optimized anyway, but need to be sensible).
        - C1: $2.2 \mu\text{F}$
        - L1: $100 \mu\text{H}$
        - $t_{on}$: $50 \mu\text{s}$
        - RL is external.
